newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian rescuers dig towards landslide survivor.
newsitem.headline: Australian rescuers dig towards landslide survivor.

text.p: Rescuers were digging with their hands in a slow but desperate attempt to reach a man found alive on Saturday in the rubble of two Australian ski lodges hit by a landslide more than two days ago.
"A miracle has occurred...," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters. "They have made voice contact with a male person and he is certainly alive."
Police would not identify the man or reveal any details of injuries, but local media named him as Stuart Diver, a ski instructor.
The man is under a concrete slab which prevented him from being crushed by tonnes of soil, rock and building wreckage which buried 20 people on Wednesday night.
Medical experts said the slab had also protected the man from the freezing overnight temperatures, which froze rescue equipment, by creating an insulating air pocket.
"Ambulance officers are in the cavity, some metres from reaching him. He is conscious and alert and talking to paramedics...," Sanderson said.
"He said he does not have a lot of feeling in his body, but he can move."
Rescue officials said they were still about two metres from the man and it was not known when they would reach him.

"...We are still talking two metres of compacted debris. The first priority is to make physical contact and we are trying to get a passage through to him," fire brigade spokesman Ian Krimmer told Reuters.
Krimmer said the passage initially was likely to be only wide enough to make contact and ensure the man was kept in a stable condition.
Rescuers said it may take hours to pull the man to safety as they delicately pull away pieces of rubble, fearing they may dislodge concrete which would crush the man.
"If what we do under there for example forces the slab to drop our efforts will be vain," Sanderson said.
"The slab is secured to the best of our ability but we're unable to lift it. It would be extremely perilous to make any effort to remove it."
A landslide entombed 20 people around midnight on Wednesday at Thredbo, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney and Australia's most popular skiing resort.
Nineteen people were buried in two ski lodges, while a woman walking home with her husband was swept away by the slide.
Three deaths have been confirmed but only one body has been recovered after more than 60 hours of painstaking digging by rescuers.
Massive slabs of concrete, where people are believed to be buried, were cautiously sawn into pieces before being hoisted free.
But conditions were so cold overnight that the water being used to cool the saws was freezing.
Rescuers had all but given up hope of finding a survivor, with the fear of more landslides frequently suspending rescue operations.
Police on Friday had virtually ruled out the chance of finding a survivor, saying the likelihood was "infinitesimally small."
But just after dawn on Saturday rescuers heard muffled sounds and detected muscle movement under one concrete slab, sparking frantic attempts to dig the survivor out by hand.
Rescuers said there was a sense of euphoria around the slide site, where about 100 rescuers were working.
Family and friends of the victims have kept a grim vigil on the search, watching from a facing hillside.
Thredbo sits on a ridge facing the snow-covered mountain range of the Kosciuszko National Park.
